episode_title: Centraal Goes Quiet, a Wine Bottle Tests the Settlement Ban, and Ladders for Toads
description: Amsterdam Centraal had no trains at all on Saturday, and service is still reduced through Monday. A former SGP MP bought Israeli wine on purpose to test the new ban on settlement goods, the cabinet's budget offer mostly pays off for PRO, and cleaners are getting ready to strike again. Also today: the University of Amsterdam's wartime apology, Demi Vollering's second title in a week, and the little ladders saving Dutch toads.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not a single train at Amsterdam Centraal yesterday. And if you're travelling today or tomorrow, it's not over yet.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Plus a former MP who went out and bought two bottles of wine on purpose, just to test a brand-new Dutch law.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's Sunday, the fourth of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. This is Dutch Daily Briefing.

segments.title: No trains at Amsterdam Centraal, reduced service through Monday

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Let's start at Amsterdam Centraal, which went all of Saturday without a single train.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's quite something for a station that handles about two hundred thousand people a day. What happened?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Engineering works. ProRail, the company that manages the tracks and stations, was connecting a new track, called 11a, and taking another one, 14a, out of service. That meant changing the safety and signalling systems, and you can't do that with trains running through.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Quick newcomer note: ProRail and NS aren't the same thing. ProRail owns the road, basically. NS, the Dutch railway company, drives the buses. Well, the trains.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yesterday people were sent to the metro, which took NS tickets. And it's not fully back yet. Today there are fewer trains between Haarlem, Centraal, Weesp, Almere Centrum and Hilversum.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And tomorrow's the one to watch, right? Monday morning.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. On Monday there are fewer trains between Zaandam and Schiphol, and between Centraal, Muiderpoort and Utrecht Centraal. Muiderpoort is the station in Amsterdam-Oost on the line to Utrecht. NS expects heavy crowding there, especially in the spits, the rush hour.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So if you commute to Utrecht, what's the advice?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Avoid Centraal if you can. NS suggests going via Sloterdijk, Amsterdam Zuid or Duivendrecht instead.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And when's it back to normal?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Tuesday, with one change. From then on, trains won't stop at platforms 13 and 14, so that platform can be widened and made easier to get to. It's all part of a bigger renovation of platforms, stairs and lifts.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That makes sense when you hear ProRail expects two hundred and seventy-five thousand people a day by 2030.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So if you're heading to Utrecht tomorrow morning, give yourself extra time, or just start from Zuid.

segments.title: Cleaners plan new strikes as employers refuse talks

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: While we're on stations, the cleaners who struck there last month are getting ready to strike again.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The union FNV says there'll be new strikes, because employers won't come back to the table. And Sam, this is really a story about two unions.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Right. Most Dutch sectors run on a cao, a collective labour agreement. It sets wages and conditions for the whole industry, whether you're in a union or not. And there are several unions. FNV is the biggest, and it leans left. CNV is smaller, with Christian roots.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the employers signed with CNV.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: On the first of September. The employers' association, Schoonmakend Nederland, did a deal with CNV that runs until mid-2028, and FNV was left out. Now the employers say a finished cao isn't a starting point for new talks.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So what's actually in it?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Pay goes up 3.1 percent this coming January and 3 percent the January after. The starting wage becomes sixteen euros an hour. And about 85,000 cleaners who never got a travel allowance will now get one.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That doesn't sound terrible. So why did FNV members say no?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: More than 80 percent of them voted it down. A big reason is sick pay: the deal cuts it for people with less than six years in the sector. FNV wants no loss of income when you're ill, automatic inflation adjustment, a bigger raise, and the same allowances for hotel cleaners.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And they've already tried striking.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In mid-September they held a five-day strike at Schiphol, train stations and universities. About 800 cleaners took part, and hundreds rallied outside the Utrecht head office of the cleaning company Asito. But Schiphol and NS reported little disruption, and the employers didn't budge.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So when's the next one?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: FNV hasn't said when or where yet.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We'll tell you once the dates are out.

segments.title: Cabinet's budget offer mostly benefits PRO

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Some of those unions are also in our next story, the fight over next year's budget.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Quick setup. The Netherlands has a minority cabinet of D66, VVD and CDA, led by Prime Minister Rob Jetten. Together they hold 66 of the 150 seats in the Tweede Kamer, the House of Representatives.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's ten short of a majority, and they're even further short in the Senate.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So every budget needs opposition votes. This week, after talks with five opposition parties, Jetten made what he called a new and attractive offer.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And what's in it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The big item: the cabinet dropped about six billion euros in planned cuts to social security. That covers unemployment benefit, disability benefit, and the AOW, the state pension.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the unions FNV, CNV and VCP called that an important victory and called off strikes they'd planned. The cleaners' dispute is a separate fight, though.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Then there's box 3, the tax on savings and investments. From 2028, the plan is to tax actual gains on shares, bonds and property. But to help pay for all this, the tax-free allowance would drop from 1,800 euros to 1,000 per person.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Which would bring an estimated 850,000 more people into that tax. So if you've got a bit put away, keep an ear on this one.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And director-shareholders could borrow at most 100,000 euros from their own company, down from 500,000.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So who walked away happy?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Mostly PRO. That's the party formed this summer when GroenLinks and Labour, the PvdA, merged, and it's led by Jesse Klaver. Scrapping the welfare cuts was one of its central demands.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: But they're not fully on board?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not yet. PRO and Volt are negotiating together. They'll back the Social Affairs budget, but they still disagree on taxing wealth and on the rest of the tax plan. Klaver wants more talks.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the right?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans called the package more left than right. He said there's nothing on tax cuts, migration or security, and called parts of the box 3 funding unacceptable because of what it does to small investors. SGP leader Chris Stoffer wasn't very enthusiastic either. He pointed to missing commitments on abortion and surrogacy. Both parties did welcome the box 3 changes, though.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And ChristenUnie basically said nobody's going to love this.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Their words were that no party will be fully satisfied. Here's the math to watch: with PRO and Volt, the cabinet would have 87 seats in the lower house and 38 of 75 in the Senate.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Thirty-eight of seventy-five. That's the narrowest majority you can get.

segments.title: Open House Day: sellers skip the motivation letters

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now to housing, and yesterday's Open House Day.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Open Huizen Dag. It happens twice a year, organised by the NVM, the big estate agents' association. You can just walk in and look around, no appointment.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: This time almost 14,500 homes took part, up from about 8,900 in March. Amsterdam had more than anywhere else, with 665.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why the jump?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: More homes are for sale. The NVM says landlords are selling off rental properties now that the tax rules for them have become less favourable. That includes the box 3 tax we just talked about.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So more homes to buy and fewer to rent. That's mixed news if you're an international renter.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. The NVM says around 65,000 people came to look. That's more than in spring, but fewer per home: about four and a half, down from almost six.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I saw different numbers on how big a share of the market took part.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes. The NVM says it was 28 percent of everything for sale on Funda, the listings site. NL Times put it at 14 percent, measured against a bigger total.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So is the market cooling?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: A little, nationally. Higher mortgage rates mean buyers can borrow less, and the banks ING and ABN Amro expect only limited price rises in the coming months. But Amsterdam is Amsterdam. In the second quarter, 78 percent of homes there sold above the asking price, by 7.1 percent on average. The average sale price was 588,000 euros, though that's slightly down on a year ago.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Okay, now the motivation letters. Explain these to me.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Some buyers attach a personal letter to their bid, about who they are and why they love the place.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Like the love letters people write in hot US markets.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And Amsterdam sellers told Het Parool they don't even read them. All that counts is the best price.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So skip the poetry and call your mortgage adviser.

segments.title: Ex-MP buys settlement wine to test the new ban

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, a wine purchase that's turned into a test of a new Dutch law.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Who bought it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Roelof Bisschop, a former MP for the SGP, the strictly orthodox Protestant party we just heard from in the budget talks. It's strongly pro-Israel. On the Christian TV channel Family7, he said he deliberately bought two bottles of Israeli wine the day after the ban on goods from Israeli settlements took effect.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Remind us what the ban covers.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Since the twenty-second of September, it's been illegal here to import, sell, trade or buy goods from settlements in Israeli-occupied territories. Like most countries, the Netherlands considers those settlements illegal under international law. Breaking the ban can mean community service, a fine, or up to six years in prison.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And Bisschop called his purchase a statement against a decision he fundamentally opposes.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Activists from the BDS movement, the pro-Palestinian boycott campaign, have reported him to the FIOD, the fiscal crime investigation service. Nobody has publicly confirmed the report was received, and a ministry spokesperson said it was too early to comment.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: But did he actually break the law?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's not clear. The winery, Teperberg, is on a UN list of companies active in settlements because it has vineyards in the West Bank. But it says this particular wine is made just outside, in Israel itself. And Bisschop says he doesn't know where his bottle came from.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Which shows how hard this is to enforce.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Very hard. Customs only checks imports from outside Europe, and only by risk-based sampling. Goods can come in through other EU countries, and most of those have no such ban. Spain is an exception. NOS even found Golan Heights wine on a Dutch-looking webshop based in Germany. Nobody checks what's on Dutch shelves, and the FIOD only acts when someone files a report.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Meanwhile, Israel is furious.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Last Sunday, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar revoked the diplomatic status of Dutch staff at the mission in Ramallah, the seat of the Palestinian Authority. He gave them seven days to hand back their Israeli-issued diplomatic papers. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen says eight staff are affected.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How has The Hague responded?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Berendsen called it unnecessary, said he deeply regrets it, and told Israel's ambassador so. He says the ban follows from the international-law duty not to contribute to illegal settlements. Talks with Israel are under way, and he says the staff's protection comes first. Without diplomatic passports, and with all those border crossings, their work would get very complicated.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And wasn't there some kind of travel warning too?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Israel warned its citizens flying to the Netherlands about long baggage checks. Dutch customs denies that.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The ban will be reviewed within a year. Between a two-bottle protest and a diplomatic standoff, that review won't be short of material.

segments.title: University of Amsterdam apologises for wartime dismissals

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The University of Amsterdam has apologised for how it treated its own staff during the Second World War.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: What happened back then?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Germany occupied the Netherlands from 1940. Staff at the UvA first had to sign so-called Aryan declarations. Then, from late November 1940, Jewish professors and lecturers were removed. Staff punished for resistance work were dismissed too. The university was part of the city administration at the time, and the city carried out the dismissals on the occupiers' orders.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the apology came this week.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: On Wednesday, when a new monument was unveiled in the garden of the Oudemanhuispoort, a historic covered passage in the city centre that's part of the university. It carries the names of 254 students and 28 staff members who didn't survive the war. Some were murdered because they were Jewish, some because they were in the resistance, some for both.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: One of the names is a professor of economics and statistics. He was dismissed in 1940, went into hiding, and was arrested in 1944. He died in Auschwitz.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The board chair, Vinod Subramaniam, acknowledged that the university offered no resistance to the measures of the occupying forces. He apologised to everyone who suffered that injustice, and to their descendants. And he said the decision should never have taken so long.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Is anything changing beyond the words?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes. The dismissals have been formally reversed. And the university is correcting its historical staff register, the Album Academicum, so that for the professors and lecturers the occupiers removed, their employment now ends on the date of their death.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So on paper, finally, they never stopped belonging to the university.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It adds to a series of formal apologies here in recent years, from the government, NS, the central bank and the city of Amsterdam.

segments.title: The Netherlands loses its Eurovision board seat

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Maya, pop quiz: how many times have the Dutch won Eurovision?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Five. The last one was Duncan Laurence in 2019. Never test me on Eurovision.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Noted. Well, the Netherlands has now lost its seat on Eurovision's governing committee, the Reference Group.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The group that oversees the contest for the broadcasters. Why did they lose it?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The boycott. The Dutch head of delegation, Claudia van der Pas, had been elected for two years. Then last December the broadcaster AVROTROS pulled out of the 2026 contest over Israel's participation. She was allowed to stay on in a non-voting wildcard spot, but that ran out this summer.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So, no vote.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: No vote. The EBU, which organises Eurovision, says elected seats are for delegation heads who are actually doing the job.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Didn't Spain boycott too?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It did. And the chair of the Reference Group is still Ana María Bordas of the Spanish broadcaster RTVE, with a term that runs until June 2027.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Very Eurovision. Nul points for consistency.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Here's the twist, though. In August, AVROTROS said it would skip 2027 as well. Then in late September the umbrella broadcaster NPO took over and said the Netherlands will compete after all, because the EBU had given it firmer commitments. NOS will broadcast it, and a panel of experts will pick the act.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And van der Pas?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: She says she's absolutely open to coming back.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So the seat's gone, but the living-room Eurovision parties are back on. And here, those are serious business.

segments.title: Demi Vollering adds the European title

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: From one European contest to another: cyclist Demi Vollering is having quite a week.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: A week ago she became world champion in Canada. Yesterday in Slovenia she added the European title.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: At this point she's just collecting jerseys.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: She rode the last fifteen kilometres on her own. Puck Pieterse took silver for the Netherlands by winning the sprint of the chasing group.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And it was a proper team effort. Sprinter Lorena Wiebes set the pace early. On the final climb, Femke de Vries and Pieterse cranked it up, and then Vollering attacked. Riders can't use race radios at these championships, so all of that had to be planned in advance.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The national coach, Laurens ten Dam, said it looked almost like PlayStation.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now my favourite bit. Two kilometres from the finish, Vollering pointed at a sticker on the back of her helmet. It's a picture of Ten Dam on a scooter in Rwanda, a team good-luck tradition.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Of course it is. And the reward?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: He's promised them burgers and good wine.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's her second European title in a row, and Dutch women have won nine of the last ten. Her season already includes the Tour of Flanders, Liège–Bastogne–Liège, the Giro and the Tour de France.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: There's one catch. The world champion's rainbow jersey outranks the European one, so next year nobody will wear the European jersey in the women's peloton.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The men race this afternoon, almost two hundred kilometres, and Belgium's Remco Evenepoel is the favourite.

segments.title: Ladders to get toads out of drains

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Maya, have you ever wondered what happens to a toad that falls into a drain?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I have not. But I suspect I'm about to find out.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It can't get out. Once a toad ends up in the gutter, it can't jump high enough to escape. So it dries out, gets run over, or falls into the drain. By some estimates, hundreds of thousands of amphibians die in drains and sewers every year.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the Dutch toad population has fallen by about 40 percent in eighteen years. So, what's the fix?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The paddentrapje, or toad ladder. It's a little strip of recycled plastic with grip, fixed into the corner of the drain so they can climb out. In trials, 95 percent of adult toads got out within a day.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I love that someone ran that trial.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Zwolle put in 122 of them two years ago. The conservation group Ravon says each ladder saves at least five amphibians a year.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And now it's spreading. Next year twelve more municipalities join, including Alkmaar, Zaanstad, Leeuwarden, Edam-Volendam and Zoetermeer. Each will get its own toad plan, with things like small ponds near schools and lowered curbs.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: A plan costs around 28,000 euros, and the project pays half, using Postcode Lottery money. It's called Pad uit de Put: Toad out of the Drain.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: If you've seen volunteers carrying toads across the road here in spring, it's the same spirit.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if you want to chip in, Ravon asks a 35-euro donation to sponsor a ladder. Cheapest home improvement in the country.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: If you're feeling curious today, it's the last day of the Weekend of Science. It's free, from ten till six, at places all over the city, from NEMO and ARTIS-Micropia to Science Park and the Trippenhuis.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: There's a mini-tornado at Science Park, and you can sit in a real Airbus 320 cockpit at the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences. I know where I'm going.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Tonight, Radiohead guitarist Ed O'Brien opens his solo tour at Carré at eight. It's his first solo show here. Tickets can't be transferred, so download the Ticketmatic app before you buy.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Or try something completely different: butoh, an avant-garde dance form from Japan, at De Lange Adem near the Oosterpark. Five dancers, eight o'clock, a ten-euro donation, cash only, and you don't need any Dutch.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And if you're catching a train tomorrow morning, leave early. That's Dutch Daily Briefing for Sunday the fourth of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.
